title: Pasco County Commission, District 2
what_it_does: County commissioners set the county budget and property-tax (millage) rate, adopt land-use and zoning rules, and oversee county services such as roads, parks, libraries, fire/EMS and utilities.
verified_ballot_note: Confirmed Oct. 18, 2026 from county sources (the state's candidate list is incomplete for county offices): Only one Republican and one Democrat qualified and there was no write-in, so there was no primary for this seat. The SOE's 2026 Local Candidates list (9/16/2026) shows Vazquez (DEM) and Weightman (REP) both 'Qualified' and no one else. The SOE's Nov. 3 results page lists exactly Seth Weightman (REP) and Stephanie C. Vazquez (DEM).

candidates.name: Seth Weightman
candidates.occupation: Pasco County commissioner, District 2; previously a regional executive for Republic Services
candidates.background: Weightman is a Pasco County native who took office as District 2 commissioner in November 2022, succeeding Mike Moore, after working as a regional executive for a waste services company. He sits on the Southwest Florida Water Management District governing board. He faces Democrat Stephanie Vazquez on November 3, 2026, in a district covering some of the county's fastest-growing area.

taxes.summary: His campaign site says he reduced property tax rates four times while investing more than $123 million in roads and sidewalks.

sources.title: Conservative Seth Weightman for Pasco County Commission District 2

property_tax.summary: His campaign site lists adding an additional $50,000 homestead property tax exemption to help seniors stay in their homes among his accomplishments, along with reducing property tax rates four times.
property_tax.quote: Adding an Additional $50,000 Homestead Property Tax Exemption to Help Our Seniors Stay in Their Homes

candidates.name: Stephanie C. Vazquez
candidates.occupation: Marketing manager, Northeastern University; U.S. Air Force veteran
candidates.background: Vazquez is a U.S. Air Force veteran who works as a remote marketing manager for Northeastern University and has been pursuing a master's degree in public administration. She has served as an advisory board member for Post 9/11 Veterans Corp., as vice president of the U.S. Institute Against Human Trafficking, and as public information officer for the City of Zephyrhills. She is the Democratic nominee against incumbent Seth Weightman in District 2.

taxes.summary: She says she would ask tough questions before approving new spending and fight for a county government that tightens its belt before asking taxpayers to do more, while also saying core services such as public safety and emergency response should be protected. She does not state a position on cutting property tax rates.
taxes.quote: Fight for a county government that tightens its belt before asking taxpayers to do more

other_issues.title: Housing and transparency proposals
other_issues.summary: Proposes a county rule requiring larger developments to include affordable homes, repeal or major reform of the Live Local Act, evening commission meetings and a Resident Growth Advisory Council; says the county should cut waste before raising taxes. Weightman did not answer the Hernando Sun's questions.

sources.title: Pasco BOCC Candidate Q+A District 2 (Hernando Sun; full text read via the site's RSS feed because the article page blocks automated access)

other_issues.title: Live Local Act and county control over development
other_issues.summary: In a Hernando Sun questionnaire, Vazquez said she supports repealing or significantly reforming the state Live Local Act so Pasco has more say over what gets built, and proposed requiring larger developments to include a share of affordable homes.

sources.title: Pasco BOCC Candidate Q+A District 2 (Hernando Sun; text read via the site's RSS feed)

other_issues.title: Transparency and evening meetings
other_issues.summary: Vazquez said she would propose evening commission meetings, clearer public explanations of major agenda items, and a Resident Growth Advisory Council so residents can weigh in before major development decisions. (Weightman had not answered the paper's questions at press time.)
